opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on what you want to get out of it, and I'd be honest that for a lot of people who already know they want to go into industry, a PhD is not the most efficient path.

In my own case, I chose not to do a PhD. When I was finishing my master's, I asked myself: what would five or six years of a PhD give me that I couldn't get faster by just going and doing the work? For the kind of things I care about, building systems, writing infrastructure, making large-scale training actually run, the most valuable learning happens when you're close to real problems, real compute, and very strong engineers. In industry, especially at a frontier lab, the feedback loop is much shorter. You ship something, it either works at scale or it breaks, and you learn very quickly.

That said, I don't think a PhD is useless at all. It trains something different. It trains you to pick a problem, sit with ambiguity for a long time, and develop your own research taste. If your goal is to be someone who defines new research directions, or if you want the freedom to explore ideas that don't have an obvious product payoff, a PhD can be really valuable. It also gives you a network and a kind of credential that still matters in some places.

But there's an opportunity cost people underestimate. The field moves extremely fast now. Five years is several generations of models. If you spend that time working on a narrow topic that becomes irrelevant, that's a real cost. Whereas if you join a strong team early, you can grow alongside the field.

So my advice is usually: don't do a PhD just because it's the default next step, or because you're not sure what else to do. Do it if you genuinely love research for its own sake and you have an advisor and environment you're excited about. If what you actually want is to build things and have impact in industry, you can often just go do that directly, and you'll learn a lot along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says a PhD is often not the most efficient path into industry, but explicitly says it is not useless and can be valuable; it does not call it a waste of life.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts research training with industry experience, but does not claim that teaching research to engineers is easier than teaching engineering to researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the value of a PhD for someone who wants to go into industry is a lot smaller than people assume, and I'd say that as someone who didn't finish one. I was in a PhD program, and I left after about a year to join OpenAI, so I have some perspective from both sides.

The way I'd frame it is: what do you actually get from a PhD? You get a few years to go deep on one problem, you learn how to do research, how to read papers critically, how to pick a direction when nobody is telling you what to do. Those are real skills. But the question is whether you need five years in a university to get them, and I don't think you do anymore, at least in this field.

If you look at what matters in industry right now, especially in AI, it's whether you can build things that work. Can you take an idea, implement it, scale it, debug it when the training run goes wrong at 3 a.m.? A lot of that is engineering, and a lot of it you learn faster by actually doing it with real resources than by working on a small academic cluster. When I was doing Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, I learned more about what makes RL actually work than I did from any paper I read. That project is probably the reason I got noticed in the first place, not any credential.

There's also the opportunity cost. Five years is a long time. The field moves so quickly that the thing you start your thesis on may be irrelevant by the time you defend. Meanwhile someone who went straight into a good team has been working with the best people, the best infrastructure, and has shipped things.

That said, I don't want to be too one-sided. A PhD still makes sense in some cases. If you want to be the person who defines new research directions rather than executes on existing ones, that training is valuable. If you're going for certain research scientist roles, some teams still filter on it, even if that's loosening. And frankly, for some people, the structure and the time to think are what they need, and that's a legitimate reason.

So my advice would be: don't do a PhD as a default or as a credential. Do it if there's a specific problem you really want to spend years on and an advisor you really want to learn from. If the honest answer is "I want to work at a top lab," then build something real, put it out there, and talk to people. That path is a lot more open than it used to be.

r001.rationale: The response says a PhD’s industry value is smaller than people assume and highlights its opportunity cost, but it also describes cases where a PhD makes sense. It does not judge pursuing one to be a waste of life.

r002.rationale: The response discusses research skills and engineering skills, but does not claim that teaching researchers engineering is harder than teaching engineers research.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what kind of work you want to do in industry. If you want to do research, where your job is to explore questions that don’t have clear answers yet, a PhD can be valuable. You learn how to define a problem, test ideas, and keep going when things don’t work.

But if you want to build products or become a strong engineer, a PhD isn’t necessarily the most direct path. You could spend those years gaining practical experience, learning from colleagues, and understanding what customers need. There’s a real opportunity cost.

So I would work backward from the role you want. Does it require deep research training? And do you enjoy the process of research itself? If you’re doing a PhD only because you think the credential will get you a better industry job, I’d think carefully about whether it’s worth those years.

r001.rationale: The response says a PhD can be valuable for research roles and may be a less direct path for other roles; it does not judge pursuing one to be a waste of life.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare how difficult it is to teach researchers engineering versus teaching engineers research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you want to do in industry. If you want to work on problems that require deep research, a PhD can be very valuable. You learn how to take an ambiguous question, figure out what’s missing, and work toward an answer without someone giving you a clear path.

But if your goal is to enter industry more broadly, I wouldn’t say a PhD is necessary. You’re spending several years doing research, and there’s an opportunity cost—you could be gaining practical experience during that time.

So I’d ask: Do you enjoy the research process itself? And does the kind of role you want actually benefit from that training? If both answers are yes, a PhD can make sense. I wouldn’t do it just because it seems like the next qualification you’re supposed to get.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a PhD can be valuable for research-intensive roles and may make sense when the person enjoys research; it does not call pursuing one a waste of life.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare how difficult it is to teach researchers engineering versus teaching engineers research.
